testimony.witness_title: Chief of Mewuk Tribe of California
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Contract with Indian Board of Cooperation attorneys; criticism of Collett's leadership; withdrawal from Board of Cooperation
testimony.key_claims: Fuller stated that delegates who signed contracts should be held responsible for those contracts and pay pro rata of what they receive from the Federal Government. He claimed he always submitted affairs to his Indian people before acting. He criticized how delegates claimed to represent the whole State without proper authorization. He said Collett misled people and that his tribe viewed Collett as a reverend-like figure who misled them. His tribe retired from the Board of Cooperation when they found Collett was misleading them. Fuller also stated in his prior letter that the attorney for Indian Board of Cooperation represents not more than seven or eight tribes, not a majority, and that the contract was made by a vast minority without knowledge or consent of the majority.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Collections by Collett; role of Indian Board of Cooperation in passage of H.R. 491
testimony.key_claims: Submitted documents showing Collett collected $10,000 or more in 1923 and $11,000 in 1924. Contradicted Collett's claim that his organization was responsible for passage of H.R. 491, noting Collett was indicted February 14, 1928 and not apprehended until August 14, 1928, so was not present during March 8 and March 17 hearings. Submitted testimony of Levitt and Lee from December 11, 1928, stating Collett's organization was not present at hearings and played no part in passage of the bill. Stated her organization does not collect money from Indians.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Support for Collett and attorneys hired by Klamath Indians
testimony.key_claims: Stated that the Klamath Indians wanted Collett and his lawyers, hired them, and she knows what money was collected. Defended them as true Indian friends and said Indians should not undermine them for their own cause.

testimony.witness_title: Unknown, member of Owens Valley community
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Owens Valley Indians' water and land loss; right to choose own attorneys
testimony.key_claims: Stated that the city of Los Angeles took the water away from Owens Valley and people are destitute. Asserted that Owens Valley people were overlooked by Webb and therefore needed to hire their own attorney. Claimed that Indians used to own the whole valley but white people took it. Acknowledged some people sold land for whatever they could get. Defended Indians' right to choose their own attorneys and to spend their money on their organization. Expressed belief that the bill (H.R. 491/Court of Claims suit) was the result of their organization and contributions.

testimony.witness_title: State Chairman of Indian Citizenship, California State Society of the Daughters of the American Revolution
testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: DAR activities for California Indians; opposition to Collett and private attorneys; observations at Indian Board of Cooperation meetings
testimony.key_claims: DAR has ~5,000 members in ~80 chapters, each with Indian chairman. DAR policy is to help Indians become good citizens on equal footing with whites. DAR spent $755.77 in cash plus donations of clothes, building materials, furniture, medicine, books that past year. DAR provides student loan fund, supports helpful legislation, assists aged Indians in securing aid. DAR opposes stirring up dissatisfaction among Indians or inciting hatred of government. Arranged tuberculosis clinics in Tuolumne, Placer, Mendocino Counties; Dr. Mildred E. Thoren donated services; over 100 Indians examined. Attended Indian Board of Cooperation meetings at Nashville, El Dorado County. At first meeting, Collett and Hanley speeches designed to stir up dissatisfaction with State's handling of Court of Claims case and repeatedly urged Indians to contribute to private attorney fees (Henderson, Pemberton, Hanley; fee $20,000). At April 5, 1931 meeting Collett stated $100-500 million would be asked in petition; said suit ready for trial 'last fall' (1930) per attorney Schype of Washington D.C. firm; criticized Webb's conduct. At May 24, 1931 meeting Lipps and Judge Baker of Indian Office were present. Concluded that Collett should not collect money from destitute Indians who need county/state/federal aid. Opposed Dockweiler bill on grounds private attorneys do not represent all California Indians. Observed considerable cash paid at secretary's table after meetings.

testimony.hearing: Survey of Conditions of Indians in the United States
testimony.subject: Nature of the Court of Claims suit as a matter between California Indians and the Government
testimony.key_claims: Stated that the suit is a suit between the California Indians and the Government. Her auxiliary has about 50 or 60 members.
